subject: living with water shortages in a rural village: buying water, boreholes, tanker queues and giving up on the municipality
citation: Seretlo-Rangata ML, Sodi T, Govender S (2025). Psychological effects of water scarcity on community members: a case study of Lephalale municipality, Limpopo province, South Africa. Frontiers in Psychology 16:1537992. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1537992

claims.text: Extreme scarcity is the baseline: when water is absent for days at a time, any offer is judged against an unbearable, hopeless situation rather than against normal service.
evaluative_rules: Judge any water solution by whether it relieves unbearable scarcity, not by convenience or preference
objections: Will this actually end the days without water, or just add another promise?
vocabulary: how are we supposed to live like this

claims.text: Water access is a money problem: because municipal supply is unreliable, households are forced into costly private alternatives, so any solution is weighed by affordability and the private expenditure it can replace.
evaluative_rules: Weigh a water solution by what it costs against what people are already forced to spend privately
objections: Will this remove the need to pay for water from borehole owners?

claims.text: Scarcity is shameful: because people cannot wash clothes and must queue publicly at tanks, water access is evaluated through dignity and stigma, not just physical need.
evaluative_rules: Judge a water solution by whether it restores dignity and removes public embarrassment
objections: Will this stop me from having to queue in public and go without washing?

claims.text: Promises are already broken: because shortages have been reported repeatedly while infrastructure stays behind population growth, any new offer is read through distrust of promises and expectations of unfairness.
evaluative_rules: Judge a water solution by whether it delivers fairly to all villages, not by what authorities promise
objections: Why should I believe this promise when the municipality has already failed us?

claims.text: Scarce water is contested: because people compete at tanks and communal taps, including with neighboring villages, any new solution is read through conflict risk and whether allocation will be fair.
evaluative_rules: Judge a water solution by whether it prevents fighting and guarantees fair sharing
objections: Will this stop people from stealing taps and using pressure pumps to take more than their share?
vocabulary: this is not fair at all

confidence: qualitative case study, single municipality, fieldwork around 2014 — mechanisms durable, magnitudes unknown
year_note: Interviews October 2020 to April 2021, Ga-Seleka village, Lephalale (Limpopo); participants aged 40-60.
